# Radar Overview {#radar-overview}

This document aims to comprehensively describe the construction and design decisions of a cost-effective radar architecture intended to detect and localize unexploded ordnance. Radar systems like FMCW or impulse radar are popular and effective, but have significant drawbacks for this use-case:

* Impulse-based radar systems require a large instantaneous bandwidth, which greatly increases the cost of a system.   
* LFM waveforms associated with FMCW radar can easily interfere with existing communications because they must maintain their linear frequency ramp. They are not frequency-agile.  
* Bandwidth and frequency coverage of these systems are severely constrained  
* Commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) options do not readily exist.  
* Due to the specialty linear VCOs or high-speed ADCs associated with these other architectures, they are typically very expensive. 

The radar architecture discussed herein has the following advantages:

* Wide bandwidth (up to 5.95GHz). This enables high resolution imaging.  
* Cost-effective. Each unit can be built for less than \$300.  
* Frequency-agile. The radar will be capable of dynamically retuning to avoid interference.   
* Wide frequency coverage (P/L/S/C-bands). This enables both high-resolution and foliage penetrating capabilities.  
* Increased speed compared to other SFCW architectures  
* Tunable parameters. The sweep speed, frequency, bandwidth, and other variables are software-reconfigurable, so the system can be continuously re-optimized in real-time.

The radar is built upon a software-defined radio as the IF panadapter sampling unit, with external RF front end circuitry to enable faster switching and wideband operation. The radar uses stepped-frequency continuous wave (SFCW) signal processing techniques to achieve the wide bandwidth, frequency agility, cost, and interference mitigation benefits. The shortcomings of the SFCW architecture (namely long scan durations) are mitigated by an external low phase noise frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) OOK/ASK transmitter acting as a local oscillator for the frontend mixer. Existing high-slew rate PLL oscillators are expensive, usually require an external VCO, and usually require a lot of development time to make operational. In contrast, the MAX41462 OOK transmitter costs a dollar, requires minimal external components, and can switch frequencies quickly enough. The chip’s performance remains to be seen, but should be good enough.  
This design decision enables cost-effective, yet relatively high-speed radar capabilities.   
Attached are some notes regarding the radar. A block diagram of the switching mechanism is included, alongside some important calculations. An SP4T RF switch pair is used to select the band-dependent directional coupler to be used. Since this device is intended to operate over a wide bandwidth, three different couplers are used, each covering a different frequency range. The fourth switch throw position has a duplicate 2.4GHz-centered directional coupler that bypasses the RF mixer and connects directly to the antenna. This is intended for reliability and troubleshooting, but also enables the radar to be used for other RF applications, like acting as a vector-network analyzer or spectrum analyzer without the additional nonlinearities and dynamic range limitations associated with the mixer.   
The other three switch positions go to their respective directional couplers and into another SP4T switch, which isolates the desired channel. A wideband mixer and FHSS transmitter form the heterodyning stage, which converts the semi-fixed intermediate frequency into the fast-switching stepped-frequency waveform. The frequency range of the FHSS transmitter is 300-960MHz, yielding a total coverage of 660MHz. This means that to enable seamless stepped frequency beyond this range, the SDR only needs to retune every 660MHz. The reason for using an external oscillator and mixer is that the SDR frequency retuning delay is very long (on the order of milliseconds), which makes high-BW ranging prohibitively time-consuming. Since the FHSS switching period is roughly 50us (@900MHz, I’m extrapolating here a little), the SDR only needs to retune every 1.65ms. If the desired bandwidth is less than 660MHz, the SDR only needs to tune once, then never again until the band is changed. This means that scans can be performed in real-time (see the chart below).   
Three SPDT switches are used alongside the three SP4T switches to select between the mixed and pass-through signal chains. Furthermore, integrated bias-tee hardware is included to multiplex DC current onto the transmission line and power an external Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA). In this initial prototype, low-pass filtering is not included. This simplifies the design and reduces cost, but may lead to increased harmonic emissions produced by the transmitter.  
Alongside the external heterodyning stage, the other improvement over the standard SFCW technique is baseband carrier generation and extraction. With this feature, equally spaced CW signals spanning the entire SDR’s bandwidth are generated in DSP before being up/downconverted by the external mixer. A polyphase channelizer in the RX DSP chain isolates each carrier and extracts its phasor after LO drift/offset-compensation with the other phase-coherent RX channel. This means that the stepped-frequency carriers can be placed arbitrarily close together, which increases the flexibility in max range and vastly reduces the number of required steps, leading to faster scan times.

These calculations give some important insights:

* With 12-bit samples, we can expect about 13MSPS sampling rate over USB-2.0  
* With 8-bit samples, we can get 20MSPS  
* Max SAR movement speed is not proportional to the sample rate (Fs)  
* Sample buffer of 128 is adequate for 1MHz steps  
* 1MHz steps means we get 150m maximum unambiguous range  
* At 20MSPS, sample buffer hold time is 1/20e6\*128 \= 6.4us  
* MAX4146X OOK Transmitter switching delay is 50us  
* With 1GHz BW and 8-bit samples, 1e9/20e6 \= 50 steps (N) are required  
* Delay per step is 6.4us \+ 50us \+ 10us (safety buffer) \= 66.4us  
* Scan period \= 66.4us \* 50 \= 3.3ms  
* SAR position granularity \= wavelength / 10 \= .0125m  
* Max movement speed \= .0125m / (3.3ms) \= 3.78m/s \= 8.4mph  
* Human walk speed \= 2.5mph

![][image1]  
As evidenced by the plot, we can expect a maximum movement speed of 28.1mph assuming reasonable parameters (300e6 BW, 50cm Range Resolution, 15 steps, 66.4us step period, 20MSPS, 2.4GHz max frequency). These parameters match those associated with Glan’s radar. The interesting advantage of using a software-defined SFCW architecture is that the radar can be continuously optimized for the instantaneous purpose. For example, the device could reduce the bandwidth, frequency, and effective number of bits (ENOB) to increase its maximum speed in rough initial surveys. Then, at locations of interest, the parameters can be dynamically reconfigured to optimize for resolution and SNR. A secondary advantage is that since the carriers are generated at baseband, decreasing the frequency step size introduces no additional hardware switching. This enables long range imaging, which is particularly useful for increasing safety in hostile UXO-laden environments. Finally, due to the superheterodyne-like architecture (external mixer downconverts to IF, the SDR goes to BB), a large frequency range can be covered. This allows the same unit to be used for both high resolution and foliage penetrating SAR.

## How It Works {#how-it-works}

Our goal is to create an image using radio waves in an effort to detect bombs and other UXO. However, since the wavelengths of interest are much longer than those traditionally used in optical or thermal imaging, the aperture required to produce an acceptable image is prohibitively high. By combining one-dimensional radar scans (“range profiles”) using algorithms like omega-k or backprojection, we can synthesize a much higher aperture. The benefit of this system is that these range profiles can be measured individually and at different locations so that a single, giant sensor is not necessary. Therefore, using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) algorithms, a sensor of any size can be used to synthesize an arbitrarily large aperture and increase the azimuth resolution. The disadvantages of SAR include the following:

* Physical movement of the sensor is required to produce images  
* Precise location information is required to coherently process images  
* Susceptible to electromagnetic attenuation (not good at undersea imaging or in conductive soil).

However, the advantages of this technology are plentiful, as it allows imaging capabilities to be achieved using very long wavelengths. Depending on the wavelength used, a SAR imaging system can have many features:

* Foliage penetration  
* Cloud/weather penetration  
* Ability to operate in complete darkness  
* Special sensitivity to metallic objects (strong electromagnetic reflectors)  
* And more

These features make it particularly suited to satellite operations because of the large movement paths and accompanied increases in aperture and azimuth resolution. Some other cool things you can do with SAR include:

* PolSAR (measure signals with differing polarizations to see how signals are reflected off them).  
  * This allows the material’s roughness or surface to be detected.  
  * It is used to classify terrain types, material types, etc.  
  * InSAR (Usually associated with satellites). Interferometric SAR is used to produce millimeter-resolution elevation maps of a planet.   
  * Multistatic SAR. Uses transmitters/receivers of differing locations to derive interesting data about an object or scene.

The simplest synthetic aperture radar system includes the following things:

* Radar sensor and antennas  
* Positioning system (i.e. a drone with RTK GNSS)  
* Compute hardware

Off-the-shelf options for computers and positioning systems are readily available, but radar sensors are typically expensive, subject to regulation, and difficult to obtain. The goal of this document is to construct a complete SAR system including all three of the aforementioned elements. If this is done sufficiently well, this system will make it easy to experiment with different signal processing techniques. Since computer hardware and positioning systems are highly accessible, this section will delve more deeply into the radar hardware required to produce SAR images.   
The simplest radar sensor involves a continuous-wave transmitter and a receiver. It works by sending out a constant-amplitude continuous wave signal, then measuring the return with the receiver. If an object moves in front of the radar, a doppler shift will be produced proportional to the object's velocity. To visualize this, consider travelling directly into this CW signal. When moving head-on towards the source, the signal will undergo a compression in the time domain. Similarly, when travelling away from the source, the signal will appear to be slightly stretched. These compression and stretching observations in the time-domain correspond to shifts in the frequency domain. The receiver can then perform a fourier transform of the received time-domain signal, extract the peaks, then determine the velocity from the observed frequency domain shift. This type of radar is well-suited for measuring velocities (in fact, it is used often by police officers for traffic speed enforcement), but it cannot directly measure the range of objects.   
To measure the distance to objects, a radar must transmit a waveform that allows the propagation delay of reflected signals to be estimated. The ideal waveform for ranging is a Dirac impulse, whose infinitely short duration provides perfect time resolution and a flat frequency spectrum. Although true impulses are impossible to generate in practice, many ranging techniques, including impulse radar, FMCW, and stepped-frequency continuous-wave (SFCW) radar, approximate or synthesize the response of an impulse through different transmission and signal-processing methods. In Fig. 1, we can see that an infinitesimally short pulse is transmitted through one antenna, reflected back from each of the targets (A, B, and C), and arrives at the receiving antenna as a sequence of pulses.

| ![][image2] |
| :---: |
| Fig. 1: An impulse waveform and its return echoes. |

If we slide the received waveform over the transmitted waveform, continuously multiplying them together and integrating as we do so, we will get a series of spikes at each of the targets’ locations. This step is called [cross-correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-correlation) and indicates when the received signal closely matches the transmitted one. At time lags that most closely match the transmitted waveform, the cross-correlation function peaks and we know that a target likely lies at that particular point in time. Since we know the speed that electromagnetic waves propagate in air and the time it took to reflect from this target back to the receiver by correlation, we can then calculate the distance to the target. The one-dimensional representation of target distances and reflectivity is called the *range profile*. Note: cross correlation is similar to convolution, except that it flips the signal backwards in time before performing the rolling multiplication and integration. ![][image3]  
![][image4]  
You may notice that the correlation step doesn’t alter the previous example’s received waveform in any way. Since the theoretical dirac delta function that was demonstrated previously has an infinitesimally small duration, its autocorrelation yields another dirac pulse\! From this realization, it can be observed that shorter pulses result in sharper cross-correlation peaks, and therefore higher resolution in range. This can be observed in Fig. 2:

| ![][image5] |
| :---: |
| Fig. 2: A longer-duration waveform and its return echoes. |

As evidenced by the figure, the echoes from targets A and B overlap because the duration of the transmit pulse is too long. After the cross-correlation step (illustrated in Fig. 3, courtesy of ChatGPT), the range profile exhibits noticeable triangular skirts on the left and right side. These skirts contribute to the decreased range resolution associated with the second radar waveform. 

| ![][image6] |
| :---: |
| Fig. 3: Autocorrelation of Dirac pulse (first waveform) and Rectangular pulse (second waveform). |

Note that autocorrelation is the equivalent of cross correlation in which both of the correlating signals are themselves. The usage of the term “autocorrelation” implies a single perfect reflector, which doesn’t modify or distort the transmitted waveform in any way. This is not possible in a practical sense, but aids in conceptualizing how range profiles are affected by the waveform.   
Recall that a shorter pulse in the time domain corresponds to a wider bandwidth in the frequency domain, and vice-versa (Fig. 4). Therefore, this means that the radar’s bandwidth directly correlates with its range resolution. Specifically, bandwidth and resolution are related by the following formula:  
$\Delta r=\frac{c}{2B}$  
Where $\Delta r$ is the minimum separation distance that the radar can resolve.

| ![][image7] |
| ----- |
| Fig. 4: ChatGPT-generated illustration of duration vs. bandwidth. |

   
These facts imply three things: Firstly, that an arbitrary waveform can be used for radar purposes. Secondly, this waveform must have a sufficient bandwidth to produce sharp cross-correlation peaks. Thirdly, a wider bandwidth source waveform translates to better range resolution.   
Recalling that the aforementioned CW doppler radar occupied theoretically zero bandwidth, it is now plain to see why it cannot be used for ranging purposes: there’s no variations in the signal properties to permit ranging by correlation\! In other words, there is theoretically zero bandwidth, so the minimum separable distance is infinite.  
For our imaging purposes, very high range resolution and bandwidth is often required (several hundreds of MHz or more). However, it is very difficult and expensive to develop hardware that is capable of transmitting or capturing these extremely short impulses instantaneously over its entire bandwidth. Therefore, engineers have developed methods of approximating these impulse responses over a longer period of time to enable the use of low-cost hardware while achieving the same bandwidth.

Perhaps the most widely-known method of doing this is called Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar. It involves the use of a linear frequency modulated (LFM) waveform or chirp that sweeps over the desired frequency range, similar to a tracking generator. It differs from an impulse radar in that it does not require the instantaneous processing of the full bandwidth. Instead, lower-cost Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) chips may be used with a homodyne architecture transceiver to mix the received signal directly down to baseband. From here, it performs a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), which maps frequencies directly to range. The cross-correlation step is performed by the mixer, which computes the instantaneous product of the transmitted signal and the delayed echo, and the Low Pass Filter (LPF) that follows, acting as the integrator. While cross-correlation is the mathematical operation being performed by this step, the implementation from an engineering perspective is called *matched filtering*. It is called matched filtering because the transmitted chirp is represented as a filter with the exact same spectral response. Thus, when an identical copy is passed through it, the filter response peaks. 

![][image8]  
[https\://www\.researchgate.net/figure/Simplified-block-diagram-of-homodyne-radar-frontend\_fig1\_319053959](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Simplified-block-diagram-of-homodyne-radar-frontend_fig1_319053959)  
FMCW is an ingenious method of achieving very wideband performance from cheap hardware, but it has a number of limitations for our application. Firstly, FCMW requires a highly linear transmit waveform. This is relatively easy to synthesize via DDS, a VCO, or even a PLL, but difficult to do with an SDR. Creating a wideband LFM waveform with an SDR involves splitting the signal up into blocks of a certain BW (determined by the SDR’s sampling rate), synthesizing each block digitally, transmitting each block, and retuning the LO at just the right time (this is the hard part) so that the waveform maintains its linear shape. This is not impossible to do (in fact, I *have* done this in a previous version of this radar), but there are simply better methods for our application.   
[https\://novelda.com/x7-radar-direct/](https://novelda.com/x7-radar-direct/)  
[https\://www\.mdpi.com/2813-477X/4/1/6](https://www.mdpi.com/2813-477X/4/1/6)  
[https\://www\.mdpi.com/1424-8220/20/18/5187](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/20/18/5187)

You need to decouple slow and fast-time profiles, with something like the Keystone transform. 

## Choosing Frequency Range: Balancing FOPEN and Rayleigh Scattering {#choosing-frequency-range:-balancing-fopen-and-rayleigh-scattering}

For our radar, we want as large of a bandwidth as possible since downrange resolution is directly proportional to the bandwidth. The formula for range resolution is:  
$\Delta r=\frac{c}{2B}$  
Since we want to minimize $\Delta r$ (the minimum discernable range bins), we want to maximize the bandwidth. However, we also want to ensure that we achieve the desired foliage penetration and operate at a wavelength that introduces an acceptable amount of Rayleigh scattering for our desired target RCS. We also want to ensure that our positioning accuracy is sufficient for the smallest wavelength desired. To summarize, the following variables influence our selection for the frequency range:

| Range Resolution | Bandwidth (F\_high \- F\_low, Higher is better) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Foliage Penetration | Frequency Lower Bound (Lower is better) |
| Rayleigh Scattering | Frequency Lower Bound (Higher is better) |
| Spatial Stepping Distance | Frequency Upper Bound (Lower is better) |
| Positioning Accuracy | Frequency Upper Bound (Lower is better) |

It’s important to define two different types of scattering:

* Mie scattering: Occurs when radar wavelength \<= target  
* Rayleigh scattering: Occurs when radar wavelength \>\> target (this is what we’re concerned with here)

Rayleigh scattering occurs at roughly 1/10 wavelength. (.43m @ 70MHz). For sub-wavelength radar systems, the target radar cross-section (RCS) increases with the fourth power of frequency. As such, we need to define the smallest target of interest, then pick a wavelength that transitions the system into the Mie region, in which geometric optics come into play.   
![][image9][https\://www\.radartutorial.eu/01.basics/Rayleigh-%20versus%20Mie-Scattering.en.html](https://www.radartutorial.eu/01.basics/Rayleigh-%20versus%20Mie-Scattering.en.html)

F \= c/2l

## Nyquist Zones {#nyquist-zones}

Important Note: for this radar, there is a difference between the instantaneous bandwidth and the total bandwidth of the radar system as a whole. The former term refers to the SDR’s instantaneous bandwidth and is limited by the ADC sampling rate, USB2.0 transfer speeds, and anti-aliasing LPFs. The latter term refers to the final synthesized bandwidth produced by processing independent signals over a much larger, arbitrarily wide, bandwidth.

For our application, we want to stay in the first Nyquist zone to avoid distortions associated with aliasing. In some applications, engineers place desired signals in higher nyquist zones to intentionally produce aliasing and allow direct sampling at higher frequencies. This is not used here.  
![][image10]  
When sampling a signal with a single ADC, we can digitally reproduce only the *real* component of the signal, and the first nyquist zone is limited to between 0 and fs/2. To avoid aliasing and unintended signals from folding over into the first nyquist zone, we include anti-aliasing LPF filters at roughly fs/2. When sampling a real-only signal with a single in-phase ADC, we need to perform a Hilbert transform to convert it into a complex analytic signal. This step is necessary to implement FFTs, polyphase channelizers, and extract the phasors necessary for SFCW bandwidth synthesis.

However, if we sample the signal with two ADCs configured with a quadrature phase difference, we can directly measure the complex signal. This is called quadrature sampling and it effectively doubles our instantaneous bandwidth. In this case, the Nyquist zone spans \-fs/2 to fs/2, and the local oscillator must be placed in the center of the receiving band. Most modern SDRs implement some form of quadrature sampling.

# Defining the Requirements {#defining-the-requirements}

The first thing to do before designing the board is define the requirements. For this radar, I decided it should be fully standalone i.e. will not require a computer to use it. For optimal control, I wanted the device to connect to a network via WiFi or Ethernet for SSH and also to run a server to stream the IQ data. The device will be writing a lot of IQ data, so a microSD card is not optimal as a primary storage device (it has poor write endurance and low speed). As such, I wanted the radar to accept an M.2 NVMe SSD storage drive for storing data. It will still support microSD for booting the initial OS (until the Pi bootloader is modified). Next, the radar should perform all digital signal processing on-device. This includes the filtering, loopback compensation, range profile generation, backprojection, and post processing. Next, the radar should include differential GNSS capabilities, preferably Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) for flexibility. As such, the radar must have an RTK GNSS receiver and preferably a robust wireless communication link to the base station. LoRa was selected for this task. To enable the device’s portability, the radar will have a MIPI touchscreen, alongside a full size HDMI interface. Additionally, the device should support fast, arbitrary bandwidth radar sensing, requiring the use of an external RF front end to the SDR for fast stepped-frequency CW radar (SFCW). The unit will be powered via a DC barrel jack.  
To summarize the radar requirements:

* On-board processing  
* Fast SFCW  
* Networking  
  * WiFi  
  * Gigabit Ethernet  
* RTK GNSS  
* LoRa Radio  
* M.2 NVMe drive  
* HDMI  
* MIPI Touchscreen  
* MicroSD support  
* DC Barrel jack powered

# Defining Board Stackup {#defining-board-stackup}

The next thing I did was determine what signals are required to build this unit, and what layers are needed to accommodate them. I usually do this before schematic capture because it is low hanging fruit and we can get it done quickly. Usually, a board of this complexity would likely use 6 layers (because of the density and variation of the signal types). However, here I am attempting to do it in four to practice working with constraints. Four layers is also incidentally the upper bound in JLCPCB before it is considered “High Precision” PCB fabrication, which comes with its own, much higher, pricing bracket:![][image11]  
I decided that the high-speed RF and digital traces will be on Layer 1, which means Layer 2 should be a continuous ground plane. L2 will act as the return path for RF (kinda like the outer shield of coax), so it shouldn’t be fouled by any traces or the like. Vias are ok, though, as long as you space them so that they don't block off large chunks of the ground. The ground should ideally have solid paths directly underneath every signal trace so that the current doesn't need to take detours which could cause EMI. L3 will also act as a ground plane, but may also have little power islands on it, because L4 will mostly have low speed signals (I2C, GPIO, etc.). As such, the continuous ground plane isn’t as necessary for these signals. However, each trace should ideally refrain from travelling over different pours. When placing a via for a high-speed signal on L1 to L4 (remember, no routing on L2 and L3), you should also place a stitching via from L2 to L3 to transfer the ground plane from L2 to L3. This should be placed close to the signal via (around .5 \- 1.5mm). If the L3 zone happens to be a power island, you need a nearby decoupling capacitor from the power island to ground. I like to think of each two layers as a pair, with one acting as a ground plane and one containing the signal traces. The reason that the ground planes are on the inside in our four layer board is because we want the high speed traces to be on the surface (where the components will be placed) to reduce the amount of vias in our board. To summarize the board stackup:

* L1: Signal (High-speed digital and RF)  
* L2 Ground  
* L3 Ground and Sparse Power Islands  
* L4: Signal (Mostly low-speed and power)

# Impedances and Trace Widths {#impedances-and-trace-widths}

The next easy step we can do before starting to design the board is define the impedances for each signal type and the required trace widths for our desired PCB type. The main signals of interest are RF, USB-2 Type-C, PCIe (for the M.2 NVMe drive), Ethernet MDI (Medium Dependant Interface), MIPI DSI (for the touchscreen), HDMI (for the external display). The impedances for each signal type are listed below. This was determined by googling. 

* RF: 50, microstrip  
* [USB 2.0](https://resources.pcb.cadence.com/blog/2024-impedance-matching-for-usb-interfaces-in-pcbs): 90, differential  
* [PCIe Gen2](https://docs.broadcom.com/doc/pcie-pcb-layout-review): 85, differential  
* [Ethernet MDI](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/snla387/snla387.pdf?ts=1784070043137): 100, differential  
* [MIPI CSI/DSI](https://resources.pcb.cadence.com/high-speed-design-resources/2024-mipi-pcb-design-guidelines-for-high-speed-interfaces-cadence): 100, differential  
* [HDMI](https://e2e.ti.com/cfs-file/__key/telligent-evolution-components-attachments/00-138-01-00-00-10-65-80/Texas-Instruments-HDMI-Design-Guide.pdf): 100, differential

Note that most of these signals are differential, which means each signal has two traces which must have the same length for each to ensure they arrive precisely in phase. The spacing between these traces determines the impedance. Independent signals should be routed 3 times the width of the widest trace away from the center (google the 3W rule). More info about routing later on.  
There are formulas for finding the required trace width based on board attributes, but my fab (JLCPCB) makes it very easy with their calculator. You just need to specify your desired material, prepreg, outer and inner copper weight, desired impedance, and reference layer, and it will give the width for various trace types. Note that this needs to be done before you route your board because you need to know how wide to route your traces. Similarly, moving to a different stackup might require rerouting. I'm using FR4 despite its loss at higher frequencies. You can pick any prepreg, but I’m using 7628\. With 7628, the traces are wider to achieve the same impedance. This makes it easier to machine and makes it more accurate because it has the same machining tolerances. Put in single ended non coplanar for microstrip and differential pair noncoplanar for the differential signals. Use the default spacing for the differential pairs:  
![][image12]  
Now we know the trace widths and spacing for the differential pairs for our required impedances. 

# Footprint and Symbol Creation {#footprint-and-symbol-creation}

Before creating the schematic, I usually start by making footprints and symbols of all parts I’ll need. For most passives and standard footprints, there are thankfully already entries in KiCAD. However, for weird parts like connectors, the CM4, or the SDR, we’ll need to make our own. I generally try to use standard components to avoid the hassle and also they're usually cheaper. 

First, what’s a Footprint and Symbol? Both are used to represent the same component, but they are used for different stages in the design. A footprint represents the physical shape and pad locations of the part and is used when doing the PCB layout. A symbol denotes a simplified model of the component (kind of like a block diagram symbol), usually contains labelled pins, and is used in schematic capture.   
For the CM4, I copied the KiCad symbol from the official published IO board reference. Pick a folder in your project directory (you can also make a global KiCad library to store components across projects) to store all your component files. For every component library, make another directory. In the root, place the kicad\_sym (symbol) file. Make a subdirectory with the same name that ends in .pretty. The footprint file (.kicad\_mod) goes in here. All footprints must be in a file ending in .pretty. You make these files inside KiCad eeschema (KiCad schematic/symbol editor) or pcbnew (KiCad PCB/footprint editor). After you create the footprint or symbol, you need to add that library to the project by clicking manage X libraries, where X is footprint or symbol. You add the path to the symbol or .pretty directory here. Do this for both pcbnew and eeschema. Make sure your footprints have the appropriate pads numbered, and that they match the numbering you made in the symbol, or the footprint pads will link to the wrong symbol pins. 

![][image13]

I will walk you through creating a symbol and footprint. This part is the MAX41461 FHSS OOK/ASK transmitter from Maxim. This is used for the SFCW LO for quick retuning.

# Schematic Capture {#schematic-capture}

After you make the footprints, the next step is creating the schematic. Follow the schematics and use your engineering knowledge to design the schematics in eeschema. 

1. I like to organize schematics in hierarchical sheets:  
   1. In the main sheet, press S to create hierarchical sheets for each block in your device  
      1. For the radar, I separated it into the following blocks:   
         1. Compute  
         2. Power  
         3. NVMe  
         4. GNSS  
         5. RF

![][image55]

2. Ideally, the main sheet should not contain any components, but rather connect the sheets together like a block diagram.   
2. Use the following keys to make the schematic:  
   1. A: Add component symbol to schematic  
   2. P: add power symbols (GND, 3V3, etc., these are global)  
   3. W: Wire  
   4. H: Hierarchical label (exposes connection outside of sheet)  
   5. L: label (only usable within sheet)  
   6. CMD \+ L: Global label (usable everywhere, I don’t use this much)  
   7. ![][image56]  
3. There are many label types, but I mostly just use regular labels (the yellow one in the above image), and hierarchical labels (the purple one)  
4. Labels are used to connect pins without actually showing any wires. It makes it cleaner and allows you to separate schematics into blocks.  
5. Use \` to show the full net.  
6. Here is an example of the compute schematic sheet: ![][image57]

## Compute {#compute}

### CM4 {#cm4}

* Using CM4-Lite because it supports microSD (no EMMC, but that's OK we also have NVMe)  
* 2.54mm header on EEPROM\_nWP and GND  
* 3x 2.54mm header on WIFI/BT disable lines in case we need to disable them  
* RUN\_PG buffered  
* RUN\_PG, RPI\_BOOT, GLOBAL\_EN in 5x 2.54mm header  
* Activity and Power LEDs

### Ethernet {#ethernet}

* It supports gigabit ethernet, so there’s 4x differential pairs  
* Magjack RJ45 connector has magnetics and LEDs  
* Electrostatic Discharge protection provided by 8 reverse biased diodes (2x TPD4EUSB30)

![][image58]

### MicroSD Card {#microsd-card}

* Sliceable normally-closed power jumper to disable MicroSD if desired  
* 4 serial data lines  
* 1 clock  
* DET\_A and DET\_B floating (with DNP resistors to 3V3 and CM4)  
* Grounded shield  
* Single-ended signals must be length matched to ensure data is received simultaneously

![][image59]

### Displays {#displays}

* HDMI  
  * 4x TMDS (Transition Minimalized Differential Signals) Data  
  * 1x TMDS Clock  
  * HDMI I2C allows communication between display and radar. This allows for things like resolution negotiation.  
  * CEC (Consumer Electronics Control) allows low bandwidth communication. Examples include volume synchronization, turning display on, etc.  
  * Hotplug allows TV to detect when radar is plugged in and start the handshake.  
* MIPI DSI  
  * CM4 supports 2 DSI interfaces  
    * DSI0: 2 lane interface (720p max), not used  
    * DSI1: 4 lane interface (double the bandwidth, uses different I2C control port), used here.  
      * Uses I2C0 (SDA0/SCL0 on CM4) for touch  
  * MIPI is the organization that creates the DSI / CSI standards  
    * CM4 has 2x DSI and 2x CSI interfaces  
    * This radar uses only 1x DSI and ignores the other DSI and the two CSI interfaces

| ![][image60] | ![][image61] |
| :---- | :---: |

### GNSS {#gnss}

This section is quite easy as it consists of only the prebuilt Unicore WTRTK-980 and DX-LR02 GNSS and LoRa modules. LoRa is included to communicate with the RTK base station. The base and rover stations will be built atop the Reticulum networking stack, which provides a unified, hardware-agnostic protocol. This framework would solve many of the issues associated with a LoRa base-station including: seamless LoRa-to-WiFi bridging, and the need to create a custom framing protocol. Since these modules have been proven to work, and this is a prototype, this revision will not use the bare GNSS/LoRa ICs. The CM4 GPIO comprises up to 5 hardware UART ports that can be reconfigured. There is often some ambiguity in UART RX/TX lines depending on whether TX is from the perspective of the host or the slave. It *should* be from the perspective of the host, but I’ve read material that differs. As such, I like to have the option of switching RX and TX lines. In this situation, the hardware UART can be reconfigured to regular GPIO pins and software ‘bit-banged’ to emulate the serial port protocol. This would result in slightly more overhead, but would result in higher flexibility. It is also entirely optional and will only be enabled if necessary.  
![][image62]

### PCIe NVMe M.2 SSD {#pcie-nvme-m.2-ssd}

* PCIe \= Peripheral Component Interconnect Express  
  * The physical interface  
  * This is the GPU slot  
  * An alternative is SATA (slower)  
* NVMe \= Non-Volatile Memory Express  
  * The protocol (often paired with PCIe)  
* M.2 \= IDK if it stands for anything  
  * The form factor of the drive  
* SSD \= Solid state drive  
  * The type of drive technology (HDD, SSD, tape, optical, etc.)

The M.2form factor is keyed differently depending on the purpose:

* M-Key (used here): Used for Fast NVMe SSDs  
* B-Key: Often used for SATA  
* B+M Key: Fits into M or B slots, but only goes up to SATA speeds

I will use *NVMe* and *PCIe* interchangeably here, because they are practically inseparable. PCIe has different “lanes”, each of which is just a differential pair. The number of lanes is denoted after the letter “x”. For example, PCIe x16 is an interface consisting of 16 different simultaneous differential signals. The CM4 only supports single lane PCIe x1 communications, but it is still faster than MicroSD (despite MicroSD having more data lines). Presumably this is because MicroSD cards consist only of single-ended signals, while PCIe is completely differential, allowing it to be clocked higher.   
More terminology:

* Root complex: The middleware between CPU and PCIe switches. This is the controller that manages everything  
* BDF numbers: Bus Device Function numbers are like the PCIe card IDs. Assigned sequentially by BIOS during startup.  
* PERST\#: Active low reset line  
* CLKREQ\#: Active low clock request. To save energy, the system only sends the clock signal to the PCIe device when transmitting data.   
* PET: Like MOSI, its from hosts POV. **P**CI **E**xpress **T**ransmit  
* PER: MISO-like  
* PCIe Gen2 x1 (CM4-supported) is supposed to provide 10W according to the [specs](https://massedcompute.com/faq-answers/?question=What%20are%20the%20power%20requirements%20for%20PCIe%20x1,%20x4,%20x8,%20and%20x16%20slots?). This figure already includes some margin, as most M.2 SSDs draw \<7W peak. As such, the same 3A regulator family used in the CM4 power system can be used for the NVMe drive. However, instead of the 5V associated with the CM4, the PCIe power supply buck converter is limited to 3V3. 

![][image63]

### Power {#power}

The power supply consists of the following modules:

* A DC barrel jack power connection  
* 7V \- 40V input voltage range (dictated by LM2576)  
* Practical upper bound is 25V (dictated by DMP3013SFV ideal diode mosfet gate-source voltage)  
* An MOSFET-based ideal diode for reverse polarity protection.  
* A 5V 3A CM4 buck converter regulator  
* A 3.3V 3A NVMe buck converter regulator  
* The LM2576HVS-X (3V3 and 5V NVMe and CM5 regulator IC) EN pin is active LOW, with 40V maximum drive level (same as Vin max)  
* 5V buck converter EN pin (ON\#/OFF) has a pullup resistor with a normally open pushbutton switch to ground. When the button is pressed into the on state (it holds until pressed again), the EN pin is pulled low, which activates the buck converter.  
* The switching frequency for the buck converter is 52kHz, which is a lot slower than the button bounciness. Additionally, the output LC circuit forms a natural debouncer, which smooths the output voltage. As such, button debouncing circuitry shouldn’t be needed.  
* The NVMe drive regulator is automatically enabled when the device is powered on, but will be GPIO disabled/enabled via the CM4. This enables low-power modes, which is useful for battery power.  
  * CM4 GPIO defaults as low and we want to enable the NVMe drive by default (allows us to potentially boot from this).  
  * GPIO EN pin goes high to disable the drive power supply (the CM4 has to consciously disable this)  
  * Truth table:

| 5V Regulator | CM4 GPIO | NVMe EN | NVMe EN\# |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | **1** |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | **0** |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | **1** |
| 1 | 1 | 0 | **1** |

* The NVMe EN\# column is what will be fed into the buck converters EN pin.   
* 5V Regulator is the regulated 5V power supply that feeds the CM4  
* The 74HC00 Quad NAND gate IC is used to implement this logic. Only two are used, so we have some spares if needed later.

![][image64]

### Decoupling Caps {#decoupling-caps}

* Each IC has at least one 100nF MLCC per IC (0402)  
* Each IC group has at least one 10uF MLCC per IC  
  * Most passives are 0402 footprint, but 10u 0402 at sufficient voltages are rare and expensive.  
  * It's good to oversize caps, so their capacitance doesn’t decrease when applied with higher voltages (\>2x the voltage is good)  
  * All 5V 10u caps are therefore 16V 0805\. These are cheap and plentiful.  
  * 10u  \+ 100n on PCIe, USB VBUS  
  * Modules have decoupling caps internally, so they're fine

### RF {#rf}

As mentioned previously, the speed of this radar mostly hinges on the external heterodyning stage and the FHSS transmitter acting as the local oscillator. See the following diagram:  
![][image65]  
![][image66]

* The SDR must have two coherent RX channels  
  * One for the loopback, RX1 (the transmitted reference signal, which is the output of the directional-coupler’s forward port). This signal is pretty strong so we don't need any amplification. In fact, if we estimate \-50dBm target strength (this is pretty strong), with a TX power of \+20dBm, we’ll still need about 50dBm attenuation in addition to a 20dB directional coupler.  
  * One for the RX2. This channel is more sensitive, and should include at least one gain stage (this is built into the SDR). To decrease the noise figure, an integrated bias-tee is used to power a Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA). The LNA will ideally be mounted directly at the base of the antenna to compensate for the insertion loss and NF of the cable and components down the line. The receiver's noise figure is mostly determined by the first active component, so the LNA is included first to present a good noise figure. The [LNA’s](https://www.nooelec.com/store/downloads/dl/file/id/118/product/350/lana_wb_datasheet_revision_1.pdf?srsltid=AfmBOoqwUdWu1Q1QgeK-HdtN5P_0wzn_wOGLzsPmXBAe0HzoCTvDLVqv) NF at 1GHz is about 1.5dB, which is a lot better than the SDR’s 8dB NF (if memory serves). To calculate the improvement you can use Friis’ noise cascade formula: [https\://lnfenterprises.com/tools/friis-noise-formula/](https://lnfenterprises.com/tools/friis-noise-formula/)  
    * Assuming 1.5dB NF, \+19dB gain at 1GHz for the LNA  
    * To illustrate the point, check out this document. It lists the ADC noise figure of up to 30dB (assume this is at the same freq. as the LNA). This is pretty high for a receiver (a good one would have maybe a few dB NF), so it’s good for demonstration.  
    * Plug in the numbers into my calculator linked above. By Friis’, the total noise figure would be 11.46dB. This is way better than the 30dB NF that you would see without the LNA.  
    * As a result, including the LNA means higher SNR and crisper images  
* It is inconvenient to provide a secondary DC power cable to power the external LNA. A bias-tee serves to multiplex 5V direct current onto the RF signal so that the transmission line can carry both. It works by placing an RF choke in series with the DC power supply to prevent RF traveling into the DC source, then placing a capacitor in front of the RF-only port to block the DC from going there. The result is that the DC has nowhere to go but up the transmission line, and the RF is contained only to where it needs to go.   
* The loopback is referencing the signal *before* it is mixed with the LO. The mixer will produce a frequency-dependent phase shift, which will skew our radar data. Fortunately, this shift is highly deterministic, and therefore correctable with a simple calibration. This should also be performed on the receive mixer.   
* The differences in trace length between the RX and TX mixers and the LO will introduce an offset in the range profiles due to the unequal phase. This will also need to be calibrated out or designed with equal trace lengths. This should also be straightforward.

#### LO {#lo}

The frequency-hopping spread-spectrum transmitter supports OOK/ASK and NRZ encoding, which is critical for using it as a local oscillator. 

* ASK \- Amplitude Shift Keying  
* OOK \- On/Off Keying (Like morse code), a variant of ASK.

It supports NRZ (non return to zero) coding, which means 1 is on, and 0 is off, with no pausing at zero in between.

| ![][image67] | ![][image68] |
| :---: | :---: |
| OOK Modulation | NRZ Encoding |

Due to these two facts, it should be possible to send a repeating sequence of 1’s to output a continuous carrier from the transmitter. The radar controller (CM4) will then simply program the frequency over I2C or SPI to enable the “FHSS” and by extension, SFCW. 

* Max operating current is 45mA, should work with other 3V3 components on the CM4 3V3 regulator rail.  
* Max 16dBm output power  
* 12pF from the XTAL1 and XTAL2 pins to ground  
* corresponds to a 6pF load capacitance applied to the external crystal when typical PCB parasitics are included  
* 16MHz, 12pF crystal is recommended  
* ![][image69]  
* 286MHz to 960MHz in normal mode, and from 286MHz–320MHz, 425MHz–480MHz, and 860MHz–960MHz in low phase noise mode.  
* ![][image70]  
* ![][image71]  
* The inductors and capacitors on the PA output are impedance matching circuitry with a LPF. This is likely intended to reduce harmonic emissions and match a 50 ohm antenna load.  
* An SP4T before and after a switched impedance matching bank would allow for widest frequency coverage.  
* Another potential option is to use a binary length weighted transmission line switching network, but I’m not sure it would work because of the junctions in the transmission line segments.![][image72]  
  * This includes switched segments of transmission lines, each at half the previous length. The network allows the total transmission line length to be modified with 2^n discrete steps (the smallest increment is determined by the smallest transmission line segment). It is similar to binary numbers, and requires n different lengths and switches. 8 switches would make 256 different steps.  
  * The goal is to create a quarter wavelength, which would match the impedances over a wide bandwidth. 

[https\://www\.alibaba.com/product-detail/OpenSourceSDRLab-New-FMC-ADRV9009-Development-Board\_1601551563749.html](https://www.alibaba.com/product-detail/OpenSourceSDRLab-New-FMC-ADRV9009-Development-Board_1601551563749.html)  
[https\://www\.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/adrv9009.pdf](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/adrv9009.pdf)

### AD9363 Fastlock {#ad9363-fastlock}

I just learned of a feature in the AD9363 (the SDR chip in the SDR I’m using) called Fastlock. Basically it’s a memory bank of VCO calibration values that can be used to retune the internal LO very quickly (\<25us, which is pretty good). If these fastlock entries were stored (each in 20MHz or whatever your Fs is increments), it could do SFCW pretty quickly. The downside is that you can only have 8 different RX/TX entries. This limits the bandwidth up to a maximum of 160MHz, which is less than desired. Apparently additional off-chip fastlock registers can be added. I'll have to experiment with Vivado for this.   
New idea: instead of going through linux drivers and python, I can fill the 8 fastlock registers over SPI from the FPGA. There is plenty of RAM (1GB), which can be preloaded with the VCO calibration data upon bootup. It can refill previous fastlock entries from the cache as its filling the current sample buffer.   
[https\://wiki.analog.com/resources/eval/user-guides/adrv936x\_rfsom/tutorials/frequency\_hopping](https://wiki.analog.com/resources/eval/user-guides/adrv936x_rfsom/tutorials/frequency_hopping?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

# SDR SoM {#sdr-som}

The first board iteration implemented the 7020 AD9363 Dev board, which exposed RJ45, USB, SMA RF connectors, and other peripherals. These are convenient, but do not integrate well as a mezzanine board. To improve the form factor of the device, it was briefly considered to assemble the FPGA and RF chips directly onto the main PCB. This would reduce the form factor of the device, but introduce risk (especially with the FPGA chip, as it is 400 ball BGA. Low yields would have been expected). A good compromise is the use of [this](https://opensourcesdrlab.com/products/opensourcesdrlab-new-7010-ad9363-mini-70m-6ghz-development-board-35mm50mm-small-size) SDR System-on-module instead. The FPGA is the XC7Z010-1CLG400I, compared to the [first](https://opensourcesdrlab.com/products/new-7020-ad9363-plutosdr?VariantsId=10322) SDR’s XC7Z020-2CLG400I. Which decreases the number of available LUTs from 85K to 28K. The FPGA is at least used to de-interleave the samples, de-pad, and for some initial DSP like interpolation or decimation. Ideally, it would also be used for things like FFT, loopback correction, and filling the TX buffer. This would reduce the required bandwidth of the interface between the SDR and CM4. Technically, we would just need one RX channel at 54MSPS/20MSPS. The TX baseband is composed of fixed carriers, which can be stored in RAM. The FPGA can perform the loopback phase correction before transmitting the RX data to the CM4. This enables higher transfer rates and bit depth, which can allow us to move faster while operating the radar and increases the dynamic range.   
The Zynq/SDR SoM will connect to the CM4 via a gigabit RGMII interface. Some terminology:

* [GEM](https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ug585-zynq-7000-SoC-TRM/Register-XDMAPS_PCELL_ID_3_OFFSET-Details): Gigabit Ethernet MAC \- The Ethernet MAC controller built into the Zynq processing system.   
* MAC: Media Access Controller \- Hardware that handles DLL (OSI Layer 2\)  
* PHY: Chip that converts digital ethernet signals into the signals for the cable.   
* MDI: Analog differential signals between PHY and ethernet magnetics  
* RGMII: A reduced-pin-count MAC-to-PHY interface using four data bits and DDR transfers.  
* GMII: An 8-bit digital interface between an Ethernet MAC and PHY, normally running at 125 MHz.  
* MIO: Multiplexed IO \- Pins connected to Zynq  
* EMIO: Extended MIO \- Routes PS pins through PL fabric  
* AXI: Connects the PS and PL in the Zynq SoM

Pins:

* RGMII TXD: The four transmit data signals from the MAC to PHY.  
* RGMII RXD: The four receive data signals from the PHY to MAC.  
* TX\_CTL: RGMII transmit control signal combining transmit enable and transmit error information.  
* RX\_CTL: RGMII receive control signal combining data-valid and receive-error information.  
* TXC: The RGMII transmit clock.  
* RXC: The RGMII receive clock.  
* GMII-to-RGMII IP: FPGA logic that converts the Zynq GEM’s GMII signals into RGMII signals.  
* RGMII-ID: RGMII mode where both transmit and receive clock delays are inserted internally.  
* RGMII-TXID: RGMII mode where only transmit clock delay is inserted internally.  
* RGMII-RXID: RGMII mode where only receive clock delay is inserted internally.  
* PHY control: The configuration and monitoring functions used to manage an Ethernet PHY.  
* MDIO: A serial bus used to configure and inspect Ethernet PHYs.  
* MDC: The clock used by the MDIO interface.  
* PHY address: A small numerical address used to select a PHY on the MDIO bus.  
* PHY strap resistor: A resistor that sets configuration options when the PHY exits reset.  
* PHY reset: A control signal that initializes the Ethernet PHY.  
* PHY interrupt: An optional signal informing the processor about link or status changes.

Since were just using one PHY chip, and the 000 address is reserved for broadcast, ill use address 1 by tying AD0 of PHYAD pins to 3v3 and the other PHYAD pins to gnd through 4.7k.

[https\://github.com/kangyuzhe666/ZYNQ7010-7020\_AD9363](https://github.com/kangyuzhe666/ZYNQ7010-7020_AD9363?utm_source=chatgpt.com)  
[https\://drive.google.com/file/d/1xqUU9khVJyclNiT0mwWsY2Mmr\_Bcir5L/view](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xqUU9khVJyclNiT0mwWsY2Mmr_Bcir5L/view)

* Write to ram through SoC PS with contents of the VCO calibration figures (Fastlock register entries) for ALL freqs spaced in 10MHz intervals (54MHz, 64MHz, 74MHz, etc.)  
* PS FIFO queue over SPI to load fastlock registers on the fly.   
* PL gpio clock to synchronize fastlocks with changing buffers. (fl\_clk)  
* 1 buffer \= 1 freq step  
* 1 buffer \= 128 samples  
* Fs \= 20msps  
* 1 buffer \= 0.000006s \= 6us  
* step period \= Fastlock recall time  
  *   \+ PLL settling time  
  *   \+ RF/AGC settling guard  
  *   \+ valid acquisition time

This will be important when we implement the PS-PL GMII-RGMII from the GEM over EMIO for the ethernet PHY chip, which will allow us to transfer data over MDI from the CM4 to and from the SDR. It will also be important when we implement on-device DSP, which will reduce the required transfer rate and improve speed. 

## Setting up the PS with VS Code {#setting-up-the-ps-with-vs-code}

The next step is to get the PS development environment set up so that we can write code for the PS. This is different from the PL because instead of writing Verilog to implement actual hardware, we can write plain C to control an ARM cortex A9 processor, which increase the flexibility and ease of development. It also runs a linux distro with the necessary drivers. We will use the PS to access the Fastlock calibration values from RAM, then dynamically load them into the AD9363 over SPI. # Developing the Fastlock Controller {#developing-the-fastlock-controller}

Now that the PS and PL toolchains are set up, we can develop standalone applications for the PlutoSDR. These run in Linux userspace on the Zynq PS and interact with the SDR hardware through Linux drivers and libraries such as libiio. There's a couple ways we could do this:

1. Continue controlling Fastlock registers over Python over USB. This method is by far the slowest, but also the easiest. The whole point of doing all this is to move away from this.  
2. Control everything from the PS: The PS send the fastlock load and recall commands over SPI to the AD9363. This is likely much faster than the previous method. However, there will be a SPI exchange for every hop, which increases the latency. Future Levi: Its faster, but not *that* much faster. Go with full PL if can.   
3. Load the fastlock registers from RAM over SPI via PS, then do fastlock recall over GPIO via PL: This is probably the fastest method because it eliminates the need for a SPI transaction for every hop. SPI would only be used when loading the registers from RAM. It also eliminates the libiio overhead. Future Levi: register loads dominate the latency, go with PL fastlock loads unless \< 8 hops are OK.   
4. Load the fastlock registers from RAM over SPI via PS, then control AD9363 fastlock recall over GPIO through EMIO via PS. This eliminates the need for complex timing on the PL side (all its doing is routing the signals from the PS to the SDR), but retains the benefits of option 3\. This is the option that I will pursue. 

But before we pursue this, we need a way to actually know when the fastlock registers are changing, and a way to measure the latency. This is pretty easy to do in the PS, with printf. In the PL, we can just add an ILA (Integrated Logic Analyzer) IP block to directly measure the digital signals. I didn’t know how to do this, so I asked ChatGPT:

* Run **Synthesis**  
* Open **Synthesized Design**  
* Find the net you want to observe  
* Right-click → **Mark Debug**  
* **Tools → Set Up Debug**  
* Let Vivado insert the ILA  
* Choose a free-running PL clock for the ILA, e.g. a `100 MHz` PS FCLK  
* Implement → generate bitstream

So we need to determine which nets control the Fastlock GPIO. The [AD9363](https://www.farnell.com/datasheets/2007082.pdf) Reference Manual. Excerpt:  
“It is also possible to use hardware control to select a particular profile if desired. The control input pins in this mode are used to select the desired profile. This mode is enabled by setting Bit D1, Fast Lock Profile Pin Select in Rx Register 0x25A and/or Tx Register 0x29A along with enabling fast lock mode in the same registers. When this is set, CTRL\_IN0 through CTRL\_IN2 select the profile (if both pin select bits are set, profiles are selected in parallel). In the system design, it should be noted that CTRL\_IN pins are configurable for other functions as well so they are not available for other functions simultaneously. “  
TLDR: Use CTRL\_IN0 through CTRL\_IN2   
![][image82]  
Now if we look at the [datasheet](https://www.mouser.lt/datasheet/2/609/AD9363-3120047.pdf?srsltid=AfmBOoo6czqAyWuXRClalY8q271JB_MwegiklbT_mS9SIWwkJKPqD4fX): “C5, C6, D5, D6 I CTRL\_IN0 to CTRL\_IN3 Control Inputs. Use these pins for manual Rx gain and Tx attenuation control.”   
Now if we look at the [fmcomms schematic](https://github.com/OpenSourceSDRLab/PlutoSky_7020_AD936X_SDR/blob/main/hardware/schematic_PlutoSky.pdf), we can create the following pin map:

| Fastlock Control Pin | AD9363 | PL Bank IO (B=Bank) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| CTRL\_IN0 | C5 | B33 J19 |
| CTRL\_IN1 | C6 | B33 K14 |
| CTRL\_IN2 | D5 | B13 R14 |
| CTRL\_IN3 (UNUSED) | D6 | J20 |

![][image83]  
Back in Vivado, I believe these are the relevant nets:  
![][image84]  
We can confirm by checking the system\_constr.xdc file:  
![][image85]  
The XDC file claims pins J19, K14, and L17 are used as the GPIO control pins 0-2. This matches except for the third one, which, by the schematic, should be on Bank 13 (a separate bank). My conclusion is that the designers made a change without updating the schematic PDF so that these pins would be all on the same bank (L17 is on Bank 33, the same as the other two). It is easier from a timing perspective to have all the control pins on the same bank. It is actually kind of a relief to hear that they are after all.   
Anyway, now that we know the GPIO\_CTL nets, we can insert the ILA. I wasn’t sure from which perspective the in/out buffers were named, so I marked both for debug:

Per [https\://analogdevicesinc.github.io/hdl/projects/fmcomms2/index.html\#gpios](https://analogdevicesinc.github.io/hdl/projects/fmcomms2/index.html#gpios), ill begin by probing pins 43:40 on the PS EMIO GPIO\_O with the ILA.

## PS-Based Recall, Store, and Load {#ps-based-recall,-store,-and-load}

The good news is that we don't actually need to read/write directly over SPI. Linux exposes an IIO (industrial IO) subsystem which can handle that. Analog Devices made a library called [libiio](https://analogdevicesinc.github.io/libiio/v0.19/index.html) which interfaces with IIO.   
Notes:

* Voltage0 \= TX1, voltage1 \= TX2  
* Rf\_port\_select A \= physical RF output port (theres muxes)  
* Initialize tx channels and parameters before creating the tx buffer  
* Interleave all channel i/q samples into a common buffer: [https\://analogdevicesinc.github.io/libiio/v0.20/libiio/ad9361-iiostream\_8c-example.html](https://analogdevicesinc.github.io/libiio/v0.20/libiio/ad9361-iiostream_8c-example.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)  
  * sample 0:  
    * TX1 I  
    * TX1 Q  
    * TX2 I  
    * TX2 Q  
  *   
  * sample 1:  
    * TX1 I  
    * TX1 Q  
    * TX2 I  
    * TX2 Q  
* Separate tx/rx buffers  
* Sample/step size should be 2 (i+q) \* num\_channels \* 2 (data is 12bits padded to 16 bits \= 2 bytes)  
* Ake tx buffer cyclic so it repeats  
* Note that the sdr has a volatile filesystem so you might need to recopy the compiled scripts after reboot.  
* If you get host key verification failed, you can fix it with: ssh-keygen \-R 192.168.2.1, then enter yes

![][image90]  
I got the 2-channel TX cyclic buffer working with baseband mixing, but got significant spurs. After int main returns, I believe the TX buffer is still circulating on the SDR. Ok I fixed the stopping, but not the spurs:  
![][image91]  
I think that the issue is that there is a non-integer multiple of the baseband freq for the buffer size. For buffer size 2048 and bb freq of 100e3 and sample rate of 20e6: (2048\*100e3)/20e6 \= 10.24.  
(X\*100e3)/20e6 \= 10, X \= 2000\. So ill try changing the buffer size to 2000:  
![][image92]  
Ok it cleaned it up a lot, but its still pretty spurry. Decreasing the filter BW doesn’t improve it. Disabling TX2 channel helped a lot (ignore center spike, this isnt from the transmitter), but we still get the image around DC. I think this is from my measurement setup:  
![][image93]  
Disabling TX1 and Enabling TX2:  
![][image94]

Ironically, TX1 is connected to a dummy load, with TX2 connected to the 2nd measurement SDR. Hypothesis: I think the rx SDR is suffering overload/intermod from the image despite the low 8dBm TX power and 30dB of attenuation I added. The TX-TX leakage from the TX1 channel is providing attenuation when it leaks into TX2 channel which reduces the spurs when receiving. I reduced the baseband amplitude of TX2, measured, then increased it to full scale. Results:  
![][image95]  
Conclusion: I think I was right. The first transmission is dramatically cleaner (this is 1/10th of the amplitude of the second transmission). We can actually ignore the image because I believe this is an artifact of my receiving SDR. Note that its directly symmetrical with the TX freq about the center DC spike. When I implement the frequency hopping, it should mirror the TX freq and move closer to the center if I increase the TX freq. You can tell it's on the RX side because it's mirrored around the RX center DC spike. 

I got the SoC PS-based Fastlock, load, recall, store, and the chunking pagination-like code working, and here is the result:  
![][image96]  
They are tones separated by 100kHz steps. This is from a single carrier at baseband with the LO continuously retuning to demonstrate it working. The above example is 1000 iterations of looping through 11 frequencies, so 11,000 retunes. It only took like 10s probably to complete, so its pretty fast. I am happy about this. I think a large part of the delay is the safety buffer of 10us I added to every tuning step. This is so the PLL can settle nicely before its retuned again.  
I measured the actual time to complete the entire loop, and it was 11272876.12us. For 11,000 tunes, it was like 1.024ms each tune. This is pretty high but includes the recall and load. Measuring recall alone, its about 152.29 us, meaning the bulk of the latency is in the load, which is done every 8 retunes. For context, when doing this in Python, the mean recall time was like 517us. So we 3.4xed the recall speed which is good.   
Here are the figures of another test:  
Fastlock load:   817.30 us/call  
Fastlock recall: 152.00 us/call  
So the fastlock load is only a little bit better than in Python (1159us), which is kind of a bummer. The recall is easy to do in PL, it's just incrementing the 3 GPIO\_CTL pins, so that can shave off like 150us/tune. But the hard part is the fastlock loading, which requires SPI, DMA, and all that stuff. To get a significant increase in the speed therefore, we need to implement both load and recall in the PL.

## PL-Based Recall {#pl-based-recall}

Ok I implemented the Fastlock recall with GPIO control in the PL:  
![][image97]  
There were a few issues:  
Because I worked on the project inside 2026.1, I wasn't able to directly import it back into 2021.1 to regenerate the bitstream. It needed to resynthesize after I updated the verilog and blog diagram because the IP needed to be regenerated. This could only be done in 2021.1. Also, I couldnt find the base project in the official repo I needed to reinitialize the project with the constraints and IP manually. But now that its done, it should be fine.  
Theres a few notes on the FPGA FL implementation:

- [ ] The first fastlock profile recall must be performed via SPI (I did it from the PS)  
- [ ] The FMCOMMS project used a different pin for GPIO\_CTL2, I changed it to the one I found in the schematic: R14.  
- [ ] In system\_top.v, I instantiated a module called fastlock\_hopper, which needs to be connected to the other IP in the block diagram. You just need to create the following ports:  
      * Gpio\_status (input), 8 bit wide vector (you can leave this unconnected)  
      * Gpio\_ctl (output), 4 bit wide vector  
      * Gpio\_agc\_en (output), 1 bit wide (you can leave this unconnected)  
- [ ] In the block diagram, I attached a constant block to the fastlock\_hopper module’s enable for debugging. Ill use an AXI interface in the future to enable fastlock from the PS.  
- [ ] I also added an ILA to the gpio\_ctl bus, which only works with sufficiently fast trigger rates (100MHz).  
- [ ] You need to resynthesize and reimplement after changing system\_top.v before writing the bitstream.   
- [ ] I used the PS with a C libiio executable to load the fastlock profiles into the registers beforehand, initialize the TX ring buffer, then do the initial FL recall before the PL controlled gpio recalled. Once this is done, the executable can be killed (ps aux, kill …) if necessary.   
- [ ] Also, after migrating the project and making some changes, I no longer encounter the negative worst negative slack timing error, which means it can probably run at higher clock rates.   
- [ ] I also changed max threads to 8 so it'll generate faster, and I also enabled incremental implementation for faster iteration while optimizing the timing. 

Fastlock Hopper module:

| module fastlock\_hopper (  input  wire       clk,  input  wire       enable,  output wire \[3:0\] gpio\_ctl);  reg \[31:0\] count \= 0;  reg state \= 0;  always @(posedge clk) begin    if (\!enable) begin      count \<= 0;      state \<= 0;    end else begin      if (count \== 32'd999) begin        count \<= 0;        state \<= \~state;      end else begin        count \<= count \+ 1;      end    end  end  assign gpio\_ctl \= state ? 4'b1110 : 4'b0000;endmodule |
| :---- |

Setting the delay:  
Change this line: if (count \== 32'd999) to change the delay. The 999 comes from this:

* The system runs at 100MHz, so the period is 1/100e6 or 1e-8 or 10ns.  
* The 999 represents 1000 periods (0-indexed), so 10us

Its important to select a delay that is adequate to ensure the PLL has enough time to track to the frequency. For example, this is with 10us delay (this is the freq. Domain btw, and its very blurry and uncrisp):  
![][image98]  
Changing it to 20us (1999):  
![][image99]  
Still ugly. Changing it to 40us (3999):  
![][image100]  
100us (9999):  
![][image101]  
I’m beginning to think my clock isn't actually 100MHz. The fastlock hopper module is connected to FCLK\_CLK0:  
clk\_fpga\_0                                                                                  10.000      {0.000 5.000}   P           {i\_system\_wrapper/system\_i/sys\_ps7/inst/PS7\_i/FCLKCLK\[0\]}  
Which should mean that it is 100MHz. So the timing is right I think. I think its my measurement setup, so I changed it:  
![][image102]  
It appears to do something more expected for the first half second or so before settling into a cleaner pattern.  The C program walks the LO initially to store the fastlock profiles. This means that the steady state (\>.5s should match this pattern in the waterfall I also noticed that some of the middle freqs are weak, which might mean that the software dwell is too short:  
![][image103]

I noticed that only the 1st and last registers are being recalled (note that this is 20us dwell time, 1999). I changed R14 back to L17 for ctl\_2 and got this. The steady state matches the initial software LO walk. This means that L17 is actually the correct gpio\_ctl pin probably:  
![][image104]  
In steady state, the peaks are at 3000, 3020, 3050, and 3056 (Even though this isnt in any register. Could be a transient/intermediate PLL state). Increasing bb freq to 100e3 from 1e3 didn't help the spurs either. Neither did changing tx\_amp to 1000\. Nor did increasing buffer size from 200 to 2000\. Also tried incrementing by 2 inside the PL, but it's the same.   
Sequence: 0, 2, 5

* 000  
* 010  
* 101

Tried changing increment to 1, then increasing dwell time to 200ms. It doesn't do anything. Until I tried unplugging and plugging in the sdr again. This time it just gives a clean carrier at 3050\. Ok I had an epiphany, I think it was just cycling between 000 and 111 and the 3050 was sustained from my previous attempt at making register 7 3050 to test. I'm adding the 3-bit profile counter to the module, and will test that next with increments of 1 and dwell of 20us. Still only get tone at 3050\. Maybe its stuck at 1010\. Fourth bit is ctrl\_3 (4 bit wide bus, but 3 bit wide fastlock control bus). Ok since its nonvolatile, I think whats happening is when I unplug it, it loses the bitstream and it remains on the last register that was loaded in the C which makes the steady tone. When i program the FPGA without unplugging it, this is the way to go, and i get this:  
![][image105]  
But it matches the C LO walk except for amplitude, which indicates that its probably not an issue with the FPGA. Im talking about the gap in the center. Adding a 1ms delay between LO steps in C does not increase the brightness of the tones in the center. I changed index 5 of the profile array, and the two dominant peaks shifted. I had chatgpt write another script to disable gpio fastlock recall and manually walk through the fastlock registers with a 1s delay:

I still notice a frequency dependant amplitude variations. I reversed the register freqs and I get about the same amplitude variations. Ok, I figured it out, its my measurement setup. It was sweep timing mismatches on my SDR and fft bin scalloping which was helped when I changed my SDR spectrum analyzer upper frequency. It divided the spectrum into an integer number of fft bins and when one fell into a boundary, it registered as weak and made an image-looking reflection at a fixed freq away. This explains the amplitude variations and signal at 3056\. Tweaking the stop and end freqs until they all show strong fixes the issue. Trying the FPGA fastlock code again with 200ms delay:  
![][image106]  
Its not perfect but you can see the lines of where each tone should be. I blame the measurement setup. I’ll try it with a real spectrum analyzer next (right now I'm using a sweeping SDR). Its clearer when spacing is decreased to 200khz:

## PL-Based Load {#pl-based-load}

### Write Commands {#write-commands}

6 bits: direction and number of bytes to transfer  
10 bits: address to write to  
8 bits: data (MSB to LSB)

### Read Commands {#read-commands}

Same as write, but first 16 bits are on DI (MOSI)

Seems to be working well. I also found that the AD936X supports up to 50MHz SPI (current implementation uses 10MHz) so we can 5x the transfer speed by reducing the clock divider to 2 (100/2 \= 50MHz). if (divider \== 4\) begin means that it toggles the spi clock every 5 clock cycles. 100/5 \= 20\. One full spi transfer takes two toggles, so 20/2 \= 10MHz. If I change it to             if (divider \== 0\) begin, it should toggle clock every 10ns, making the 50MHz clock. The conditional is extraneous, but ill keep it so we can adjust the clock frequency easily in the future. The result is a 5x increased transfer:  
![][image111]

Now we need to figure out where to write the profiles too, and in what format. I found the following information about using BBP (baseband processor, the FPGA in our case)-stored profiles:  
![][image112]  
AD9361\_fastlock\_load is a driver function, meaning that the reference manual intends this to be done from the PS-based embedded linux running libiio. I just need to figure out how to implement this rawly in the PL. Probably the easiest way is just to check out the [ad9361 no-OS drivers](https://github.com/analogdevicesinc/no-OS/blob/main/drivers/rf-transceiver/ad9361/ad9361.h).   
RX:

| \#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_SETUP			 0x25A /\* Rx Fast Lock Setup \*/\#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_SETUP\_INIT\_DELAY	 0x25B /\* Rx Fast Lock Setup Init Delay \*/\#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_ADDR		 0x25C /\* Rx Fast Lock Program Addr \*/\#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_DATA		 0x25D /\* Rx Fast Lock Program Data \*/\#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_READ		 0x25E /\* Rx Fast Lock Program Read \*/\#define REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CTRL		 0x25F /\* Rx Fast Lock Program Control \*/ |
| :---- |

TX:

| \#define REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_SETUP\_INIT\_DELAY	 0x29B /\* Tx Fast Lock Setup Init Delay \*/\#define REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_ADDR		 0x29C /\* Tx Fast Lock Program Addr \*/\#define REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_DATA		 0x29D /\* Tx Fast Lock Program Data \*/\#define REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_READ		 0x29E /\* Tx Fast Lock Program Read \*/\#define REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CTRL		 0x29F /\* Tx Fast Lock Program Ctrl \*/ |
| :---- |

| Function | RX address | TX address |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fast Lock Setup | `0x25A` | `0x29A` |
| Fast Lock Setup Init Delay | `0x25B` | `0x29B` |
| Fast Lock Program Addr | `0x25C` | `0x29C` |
| Fast Lock Program Data | `0x25D` | `0x29D` |
| Fast Lock Program Read | `0x25E` | `0x29E` |
| Fast Lock Program Control | `0x25F` | `0x29F` |

[More info](https://ez.analog.com/rf/wide-band-rf-transceivers/design-support/f/q-a/100519/ad9361-fastlock-profile-loading-related-questions)

UG570 of [Reference Manual](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/user-guides/AD9361_Reference_Manual_UG-570.pdf)

| int32\_t ad9361\_fastlock\_load(struct ad9361\_rf\_phy \*phy, bool tx,			     uint32\_t profile, uint8\_t \*values){	uint32\_t offs \= 0;	int32\_t i, ret \= 0;	uint8\_t buf\[4\];	dev\_dbg(\&phy-\>spi-\>dev, "%s: %s Profile %"PRIu32":",		\_\_func\_\_, tx ? "TX" : "RX", profile);	if (tx)		offs \= REG\_TX\_FAST\_LOCK\_SETUP \- REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_SETUP;	buf\[0\] \= values\[0\];	buf\[1\] \= RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_ADDR(profile) | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_WORD(0);	ad9361\_spi\_writem(phy-\>spi, REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_DATA \+ offs, buf, 2);	for (i \= 1; i \< RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_CONFIG\_WORD\_NUM; i++) {		buf\[0\] \= RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_WRITE | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CLOCK\_ENABLE;		buf\[1\] \= 0;		buf\[2\] \= values\[i\];		buf\[3\] \= RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_ADDR(profile) | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_WORD(i);		ad9361\_spi\_writem(phy-\>spi, REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CTRL \+ offs, buf, 4);	}	ad9361\_spi\_write(phy-\>spi, REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CTRL \+ offs,			 RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_WRITE | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CLOCK\_ENABLE);	ad9361\_spi\_write(phy-\>spi, REG\_RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CTRL \+ offs, 0);	phy-\>fastlock.entry\[tx\]\[profile\].flags \= FASTLOOK\_INIT;	phy-\>fastlock.entry\[tx\]\[profile\].alc\_orig \= values\[15\];	phy-\>fastlock.entry\[tx\]\[profile\].alc\_written \= values\[15\];	return ret;} |
| :---- |

Notes

* TX addr \- RX addr \= 0x40  
* So the rest of the function can use RX register names  
* 0011 0000 \= 0x30  
* RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_WORD(x) \=  (((x) & 0xF) \<\< 0\) /\* Configuration Word \<3:0\> \*/  
* Basically makes X into a four bit word  
* So the FL RAM address is a 4-bit number from 0-8 with another 4 zeroes after it  
* *Values* is the 16-byte fastlock profile payload  
* Start at 0x25D with two bytes lets it transfer data, then address (multi-byte SPI protocol)  
* Send first byte into PROGRAM\_DATA  
* For each data byte (theres 16 of them), do this  
  * RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_WRITE | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROGRAM\_CLOCK\_ENABLE  
    * This makes 0b10 | 0b01 \= 0b11 \= 0x03  
    * Goes into PROGRAM\_CTRL  
  * PROGRAM\_READ \= 0x0  
  * PROGRAM\_DATA \= current fastlock data byte (starting from second)  
  * PROGRAM\_ADDR \= RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_ADDR(profile) | RX\_FAST\_LOCK\_PROFILE\_WORD(i);  
    * (((x) & 0x7) \<\< 4\) | (((i) & 0xF) \<\< 0\)  
    * d c b a  \-\> 0 c b a d c b a   
  * Send all four bytes over SPI transaction (into PROGRAM\_CTL)  
* Finally, there's 2 24-bit control writes per load:  
  * 0b11 \= 0x03 (into PROGRAM\_CTL)  
  * 0b00 \= 0x00 (also into PROGRAM\_CTL)

First, before each fastlock load, a 2-byte command is sent via SPI. It contains the first data byte:

| Byte | 1 | 2 |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Register | 0x25D/0x29D  | 0x25C/0x29C  |
| Register Name | Data | Address |
| Content | **0xAB** | **0x30** |

For each next byte in the fastlock profile load, this is sent over SPI (example, profile address 3, 1st data byte). Red \= iteration dependant, Black \= hardcoded:

| Byte | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Register | 0x25F/0x29F  | 0x25E/0x29E  | 0x25D/0x29D  | 0x25C/0x29C  |
| Register Name | Control | Read | Data | Address |
| Content | **0x03** | **0x00** | **0xAB** | **0x31** |

Therefore, the total number of *payload* bytes are (15\*4 \+ 1\*2) \* 8 \= 496\. Each SPI burst also has some overhead (16 bits).

| \#include \<fcntl.h\>\#include \<stdint.h\>\#include \<stdio.h\>\#include \<sys/mman.h\>\#include \<unistd.h\>\#define BRAM\_BASE 0x40000000\#define BRAM\_MAP\_SIZE 4096\#define NUM\_PROFILES 100\#define PROFILE\_SIZE 16int main(void){    printf("Writing BRAM\\n");    uint8\_t profiles\[NUM\_PROFILES\]\[PROFILE\_SIZE\] \= {0};    int fd \= open("/dev/mem", O\_RDWR | O\_SYNC);    volatile uint8\_t \*bram \= mmap(NULL, BRAM\_MAP\_SIZE, PROT\_READ | PROT\_WRITE, MAP\_SHARED, fd, BRAM\_BASE);    for (int p \= 0; p \< NUM\_PROFILES; p++)        for (int i \= 0; i \< PROFILE\_SIZE; i++)            bram\[p \* PROFILE\_SIZE \+ i\] \= profiles\[p\]\[i\];    printf("BRAM contents:\\n");    for (int p \= 0; p \< NUM\_PROFILES; p++) {        printf("Profile %d: ", p);        for (int i \= 0; i \< PROFILE\_SIZE; i++)            printf("%02X ", bram\[p \* PROFILE\_SIZE \+ i\]);        printf("\\n");    }    munmap((void \*)bram, BRAM\_MAP\_SIZE);    close(fd);    return 0;} |
| :---- |
