This confirms that the AXI BRAM interface is working, and we can now begin working on the BRAM \- PL interface. Again, the purpose of this is to load profiles from the PS into the PL’s BRAM so the Fastlock FSM can load them quickly into the AD9361’s registers.

### PL BRAM Read {#pl-bram-read}

The next step is to read the BRAM from within the PL’s FSM. The BRAM resides in PL, so we don’t need an AXI interface to read from it. We just need to write the desired address on the address bus, wait a number of clock cycles, then retrieve the data.

1. I started by creating a new Verilog source called bram\_read.v. Right now the sources look like this:  
   ![][image121]  
2. I previously initialized the BRAM address range as 32 bits wide (will be changed later to the FL profile word width), with 8192 words. Therefore the address bus should contain log2(8192) \= 13 bits. I’m using 20MSPS complex sampling, which gives 20MHz SDR bandwidth, and want a max of 6GHz BW. 6e9/20e6 \= 300 possible different fastlock calibration values / tuning steps. ceil(log2(300)) \= 9 bits necessary for the *profile\_index* register. There are 16 words in each fastlock profile, so Ill need log2(16) \= 4 bits for the *word\_index* register. So we need 9+4 \= 13 bits total for a BRAM read:

| module bram\_read(    input wire clk,    input wire enable,    input wire \[8:0\] profile\_index,    input wire \[3:0\] word\_index, (\* X\_INTERFACE\_IGNORE \= "true" \*)     input wire \[31:0\] bram\_data,    output reg \[15:0\] profile\_word, (\* X\_INTERFACE\_IGNORE \= "true" \*)     output reg \[12:0\] addr,    output reg busy,    output reg valid);reg \[2:0\] delay\_count \= 0;always @(posedge clk) begin    valid \<= 0;    if (enable && \!busy) begin        addr \<= {profile\_index, word\_index};        delay\_count \<= 0;        busy \<= 1;    end else if (busy) begin        if (delay\_count \== 3) begin        // Waits for 4 clock cycles before data is valid            profile\_word \<= bram\_data\[15:0\];            busy \<= 0;            valid \<= 1;        end else begin            delay\_count \<= delay\_count \+ 1;        end    endendinitial begin    addr \= 0;    busy \= 0;    valid \= 0;    profile\_word \= 0;endendmodule |
| :---- |

3. Next, this needs to be added as an RTL module in the block diagram. When I added this as a module, Vivado auto-inferred each bram\_data line as an individual bus, so I added: (\* X\_INTERFACE\_IGNORE \= "true" \*) before the bram\_data and addr register declaration. This makes a nice lil block like this:  
   ![][image122]

4. I then added a constant with value of 1 to the enable line and connected clk to the global clock line. 

![][image123]2

### Testing the PL BRAM Read RTL {#testing-the-pl-bram-read-rtl}

Open the Radar Vivado project, then add a new simulation source \-\> sim\_1, with the following test bench. You also need to set the bram\_read\_tb.v as top in sources. Basically, this tests the read signals before actually implementing it in hardware:

| \`timescale 1ns / 1psmodule bram\_read\_tb;reg clk \= 0;reg enable \= 0;reg \[8:0\] profile\_index \= 0;reg \[3:0\] word\_index \= 0;reg \[31:0\] bram\_data \= 0;wire \[15:0\] profile\_word;wire \[12:0\] addr;wire busy;wire valid;bram\_read dut(    .clk(clk),    .enable(enable),    .profile\_index(profile\_index),    .word\_index(word\_index),    .bram\_data(bram\_data),    .profile\_word(profile\_word),    .addr(addr),    .busy(busy),    .valid(valid));always \#5 clk \= \~clk;initial begin    \#20;    profile\_index \= 9'd5;    word\_index \= 4'd3;    enable \= 1;    \#10;    enable \= 0;    \#10;    bram\_data \= 32'h0000ABCD;    \#100;    profile\_index \= 9'd20;    word\_index \= 4'd12;    enable \= 1;    \#10;    enable \= 0;    \#10;    bram\_data \= 32'h00001234;    \#100;    \$finish;endendmodule |
| :---- |

![][image124]  
![][image125]

| Pin | Direction | Width | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `clk` | Input | 1 | Clock for the BRAM read logic |
| `enable` | Input | 1 | Starts a BRAM read when asserted and `busy = 0` |
| `profile_index` | Input | 9 | Selects one of up to 512 fastlock profiles |
| `word_index` | Input | 4 | Selects one of 16 words within the selected profile |
| `bram_data` | Input | 32 | Data returned from BRAM Port B |
| `profile_word` | Output | 16 | Lower 16 bits of the BRAM word after the read completes |
| `addr` | Output | 32 | BRAM address generated from `{profile_index, word_index}` |
| `busy` | Output | 1 | High while a BRAM read transaction is in progress |
| `valid` | Output | 1 | Pulses high for one clock when `profile_word` is valid |

# Layout {#layout}

The following table is AI-generated (*ChatGPT*, 2026), but it provides an excellent breakdown of each signal’s special considerations:

| Interface | Additional requirements |
| :---: | ----- |
| **50 Ω RF microstrip** | Minimize bends and vias; use gradual bends or two 45° bends; maintain constant ground reference; use ground-via fencing where appropriate; account for connector launches, pads, solder mask, component pads and via inductance; keep RF away from digital and switching-power sections. At microwave frequencies, validate the entire launch, not just the straight trace. |
| **USB 2.0 HS** | Route D+/D− together, short and symmetrical; minimize stubs; place ESD protection close to the connector with low-capacitance parts; avoid routing through USB connector breakout asymmetrically. TI guidance commonly permits considerably more skew than PCIe, but keeping mismatch under roughly **50 mil / 1.27 mm** is a safe conservative target. USB 2.0 is specified around 90 Ω differential. ([E2E China](https://e2echina.ti.com/cfs-file/__key/telligent-evolution-components-attachments/13-106-00-00-00-00-33-10/USB-2.0-Board-Design-and-Layout-Guidelines.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **PCIe Gen2** | Very strict intra-pair matching and discontinuity control; minimize vias; remove or avoid via stubs when long; place TX AC-coupling capacitors according to the endpoint/root-complex datasheet; preserve capacitor-pad symmetry; do not match TX pair length to RX pair length; route the 100 MHz reference clock according to its separate topology and termination requirements. A common conservative intra-pair target is **≤5 mil / 0.127 mm**. ([Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/slaae45?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Ethernet MDI** | Keep the PHY-to-magnetics section short; route each pair symmetrically; separate different MDI pairs to limit crosstalk; place termination parts exactly as the PHY datasheet specifies; keep magnetics and RJ45 shield/chassis-ground strategy correct; avoid copper beneath isolation regions when required. For gigabit Ethernet, TI recommends pair matching around **20 mil** and short MDI routing. ([Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/snla387?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **MIPI CSI/DSI D-PHY** | Match P/N within each lane tightly; also obey lane-to-clock and lane-to-lane matching limits from the processor/display/camera datasheets; minimize vias and connectors; keep LP-mode loading low; avoid high-capacitance ESD parts. MIPI requirements are highly device-dependent, so the SoC hardware guide is the controlling document. ([NXP](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/application-note/AN13573.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **HDMI** | Match P/N tightly within every TMDS pair; also control skew among the clock and data lanes according to the transmitter datasheet; minimize connector and ESD discontinuities; use very-low-capacitance HDMI-rated ESD protection; route DDC, CEC, HPD and \+5 V according to their separate electrical requirements. Older NXP guidance uses **±5 mil intra-pair matching** as a conservative target. ([NXP Community](https://community.nxp.com/pwmxy87654/attachments/pwmxy87654/imx-processors/120292/1/IMX6DQ6SDLHDG.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |

Laying out the PCB is usually harder as you go because the existing traces get in the way and you have to work around them. What I usually do is rank the signals from tightest to loosest requirements, then start with the hard ones. My qualitative ranking is this:

* PCIe Gen2  
* RF  
* HDMI  
* MIPI CSI/DSI  
* Gigabit Ethernet MDI  
* USB 2.0

# 7/23/26 Log {#7/23/26-log}

Today I’m focusing on implementing SFCW with fastlock, and obtaining at least two high quality results. We don’t have a working rail, and I don’t want to spend all day moving a radar so I’ll use the lowest frequency possible to obtain our scans. This means the wavelength is higher, so I can move it a longer distance between scans. Ill use F \= c/2l to determine the lowest frequency. I want to image a roughly .5m tall trash can so ill use 300MHz lowest frequency, with a 300MHz BW. Therefore 600MHz max freq or .5m wavelength. lambda/10 is generally considered a good granularity, so I’ll target 5cm steps. (R\*lambda)/D. We’ll say R \= 4m, lambda \= 1m, and D \= 1m (20 scans). We should get an azimuth resolution of 4m. On second thought, I think ill use 40 scans at 10cm spacing. Synthetic aperture would be 3.9m, and azimuth resolution is between .5m and 1m.  
Python file is called: fast\_scan.py

Pseudocode:

* **Generate freq step vector (center freqs), separated by fs-1e6 (ie 19MHz)**  
* **Set sdr params (gain, bw, fs, etc.)**  
* **Generate bb signal**  
  * **e^(-2j\*pi\*bb\_freq\*buffer\_vector) for bb\_freq in range(1e6, fs-1e6, 1e6)**  
  * **Buffer\_vector is basically t**  
  * **Basically a bunch of CW signals spaced evenly in baseband**  
  * **Saved as complex64 numpy**  
* **Generate global empty rx / lb (loopback) buffer arrays (128 samples wide)**  
* **Generate fastlock profiles for each frequency, then store them in Python array**  
* LOOP to generate S:  
  * **Read one rx sample buffer**  
  * **Read one loopback sample buffer**  
  * **Coherently average each channel for n repetitions**  
  * **Remove phase offset: rx / (loopback \+ 1e-12)**  
  * Each frequency is now a phasor, append these to S   
* S is now an array of phasors, each entry is the phasor at one frequency  
* S \-= mean(S)  
* Window S (optional)  
* IFFT S, n \= number of frequency steps  
* Convert this range profile to dB  
* Save this range profile to the npz file.   
* Once all range profiles have been generated, do backprojection and post processing.

# Costas Array Ambiguity Mitigation (AI Generated Documentation)

Costas Array Ambiguity Mitigation in the SFCW Radar

1. Purpose

I implemented Costas-array frequency ordering to reduce the structured range–Doppler ambiguity associated with a conventional linear stepped-frequency sweep.

In a linear SFCW sweep, frequency increases uniformly with acquisition time. A moving target introduces a time-dependent phase shift while the radar measures the frequency response. Because frequency and time are linked, this motion-induced phase can resemble the phase slope produced by propagation delay. This can shift or distort the reconstructed range profile.

My implementation changes the order in which frequency blocks are measured while preserving their correct frequency positions during reconstruction. The goal is to make motion-induced errors less likely to combine into a coherent false range response.

This is ambiguity mitigation, not a complete Doppler-compensation algorithm.

2. Generating the Costas Array

I used the Welch construction to generate the frequency-step permutation.

For a prime number p, I search for a primitive root g modulo p. The sequence is then:

a\[k\] \= (g^k mod p) − 1, for k \= 0, 1, …, p − 2

The subtraction converts the sequence into zero-based indices suitable for indexing Python arrays.

In my welch() function, each candidate g is tested by generating its modular powers. If the sequence contains p − 1 distinct values, the candidate is accepted:

for g in range(2, p):  
seq \= \[pow(g, k, p) for k in range(p \- 1)\]  
if len(set(seq)) \== p \- 1:  
return g, \[x \- 1 for x in seq\]

For example, p \= 7 and g \= 3 produce:

Frequency-block order: \[0, 2, 1, 5, 3, 4\]

Instead of measuring six frequency blocks in ascending order, the radar measures them using this permutation.

A Costas array has distinct displacement vectors between its points in the time–frequency grid. This reduces repeated time–frequency relationships that can produce strong ambiguity sidelobes in an ideal frequency-hopping waveform.

3. Matching the Array Length to the Sweep

A Welch Costas array contains p − 1 entries. My generate\_costas\_array() function selects the smallest prime in a predefined list that is greater than the requested number of LO retunes.

If the resulting array contains more entries than the original sweep, I extend the LO frequency list in increments of Fs. I then update the number of retunes, total frequency samples, and nominal bandwidth.

This means Costas mode can increase the sweep bandwidth rather than simply reorder the originally requested frequencies. The extended frequencies must remain within the hardware and antenna operating limits.

The implementation also calculates the inverse permutation:

self.descramble\_order \= np.argsort(self.step\_order)

This provides a way to recover ascending frequency order from the hopping sequence.

4. Applying the Order During Acquisition

My radar measures multiple baseband tones at each LO setting. Therefore, the Costas permutation operates on LO frequency blocks—not on every individual tone.

With the current default settings:

Fs \= 20 MHz

Baseband tone spacing \= 2 MHz

Tones per LO setting \= 10

The tones within each block remain in their normal frequency order. Only the order of the LO blocks changes.

After generating the Costas permutation, I reorder the LO frequency list:

self.FREQS \= self.FREQS\[self.step\_order\]

The RX and TX fastlock profiles correspond to this acquisition order, allowing both local oscillators to follow the same hopping schedule.

The costas\_mode option controls this behavior. When disabled, the radar uses a linear frequency-step order.

5. Restoring Frequency Order Before Range Reconstruction

Changing acquisition order is only useful if the measurements are placed back into their correct frequency positions before computing the range profile.

During a sweep, I use the Costas index to select the destination block in the complex frequency-response array:

start \= self.step\_order\[count\] \* self.num\_freqs  
stop \= start \+ self.num\_freqs  
self.S\[start\] \= phasors

Consequently, the radar acquires frequency blocks in Costas order, but self.S contains the completed response in ascending frequency order.

I then reconstruct the range profile by:

1. Removing the mean complex frequency response.  
2. Applying a Hann window.  
3. Computing the inverse FFT.

This preserves the standard SFCW range-reconstruction process while changing the relationship between acquisition time and frequency.

The later PS controller implementation preserves the same block-placement logic on the host.

6. Comparing Costas and Linear Stepping

I also added CostasVsLinear.py to compare the two acquisition orders using a moving fan.

The comparison uses the same frequency blocks for both modes, so differences are not caused by unequal bandwidth. It alternates which mode runs first on successive paired trials to reduce acquisition-order bias.

For each mode, the script subtracts the mean complex range profile across trials to emphasize changing returns. It then compares:

• Dynamic target-to-background contrast

• Variation in the target’s peak range bin

• Sweep acquisition time

The range bins are intentionally uncalibrated in this experiment. These measurements provide an empirical comparison, but they do not directly measure the full delay–Doppler ambiguity function or establish an improvement without recorded results.

7. Limitations and Interpretation

Costas ordering does not increase the fundamental unambiguous range set by frequency spacing:

R\_unambiguous \= c / (2 × Δf)

With Δf \= 2 MHz, the nominal unambiguous range is approximately 75 m.

It also does not remove target motion during a sweep. Its purpose is to disrupt the regular time–frequency relationship that makes motion errors strongly structured under linear stepping.

The implementation applies Costas ordering at the frequency-block level, so the ambiguity behavior of the complete multitone waveform is not identical to that of an ideal single-tone Costas waveform.

Finally, the larger-array fallback uses Euler’s polynomial to generate candidate primes. Those candidates should be explicitly checked for primality before extending the implementation to arbitrary sweep sizes.

8. Implementation Reference

The original implementation is recorded in commit:

0ad096f9 — “before c sfcw timing integration”

Main implementation:  
Processing/Acquisition/SFCW/SFCW.py

Comparison experiment:  
Processing/Acquisition/SFCW/CostasVsLinear.py

Key Design Principle

Acquire frequency blocks in Costas order, then restore ascending frequency order before range reconstruction.

* Improved spectral purity by making buffer size an integer multiple of num samps for lowest baseband freq. Higher freqs are multiples of the fundamental.

* Added complex least squares gain estimate / least squares loopback normalization instead of pointwise sample by sample loopback normalization. This was a huge difference, range profile stability improved dramatically.

# Schroeder Phase Complexes

| fs \= 20e6buff\_size \= 400spacing \= 1e6t \= np.arange(0, buff\_size, 1\) / fstones \= np.arange(-fs/2, fs/2, spacing)buff \= np.zeros(buff\_size, dtype=np.complex128)for n, f in enumerate(tones):   phi \= 0   buff \+= np.exp(1j \* (2 \* np.pi \* f \* t \+ phi))ibuff, qbuff \= buff.real, buff.imagplt.plot(t, buff.real) |
| :---- |

With universal starting phase of 0, we get this time domain waveform:  
![][image141]  
As you can see the crest factor is very high, with the peak amplitude much higher than the average amplitude. This is bad because we have a finite dynamic range with real RF components. The plan is to implement the schroeder phase formula to average this out. This should apply a certain phase offset to each baseband tone, which should reduce the crest factor:  
![][image142]

| fs \= 20e6buff\_size \= 400spacing \= 1e6t \= np.arange(0, buff\_size, 1\) / fstones \= np.arange(-fs/2, fs/2, spacing)buff \= np.zeros(buff\_size, dtype=np.complex128)c \= 0for n, f in enumerate(tones):   phi \= \-np.pi\*n\*(n-1)/len(tones) \+ c   buff \+= np.exp(1j \* (2 \* np.pi \* f \* t \+ phi))ibuff, qbuff \= buff.real, buff.imagplt.plot(t, buff.real) |
| :---- |

![][image143]  
As you can see it reduced the peak from 20 to 6.08 (magnitude), or 3.30x. 

# AI Git Branch

On 10/1, I decided to split the Git repository into separate human-generated and AI-generated branches so I can develop my own implementation while the AI works on the same problems independently. The human-generated branch starts at commit 0ad096f9, “before c sfcw timing integration,” which includes my Costas-array ordering and Schroeder-phase implementation. The AI-generated branch starts at the later commit da4732c4, “basic c timing controller done,” which includes the AI-assisted PS C controller integration. Each branch has its own working directory, allowing parallel development without either side overwriting the other’s changes. This separation lets me understand and take ownership of every new change on my branch while comparing my approach with the AI’s implementation. Changes can be reviewed and selectively incorporated later rather than automatically merged.
